nameStory: This willowherb gets its "downy" name from the soft, fuzzy hairs that cover its stems and leaves, giving the whole plant a velvety texture. The "willowherb" part comes from its narrow leaves that resemble those of willow trees, though it's not related to willows at all. Early botanists noticed this leaf similarity and the name stuck.
description: Downy willowherb is a modest wildflower that grows 1-3 feet tall in wet places throughout New England. It produces small pink or white flowers with four petals from summer into fall, followed by distinctive seedpods that split open to release fluffy, cotton-like seeds. The entire plant has a soft, fuzzy texture from tiny hairs covering the stems and leaves. It's part of the evening primrose family, though it blooms during the day.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small pink or white flowers about 1/4 inch across with four rounded petals and eight stamens. Flowers grow in clusters at the top of stems and have a sweet, subtle fragrance.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, lance-shaped leaves arranged oppositely on lower stem, alternately higher up. Feel distinctly soft and velvety due to dense, short hairs covering both surfaces.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Upright stems 1-3 feet tall, often branching near the top. Entire plant feels noticeably fuzzy when touched, like soft felt fabric.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Long, slender capsules that split into four parts, releasing seeds with white, cottony tufts that float on the breeze like tiny parachutes.

habitat: Look for downy willowherb in wet meadows, marshy areas, stream banks, and roadside ditches throughout New England. It prefers consistently moist soil and can tolerate partial shade, often growing alongside sedges, rushes, and other moisture-loving plants. You'll rarely find it in dry upland areas.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge as fuzzy rosettes of soft leaves close to the ground. The downy texture is already noticeable on new growth.
seasonality.summer: Flowering begins in mid-summer with small pink or white blooms continuing into late summer. Plants reach full height and the fuzzy stems are most apparent.
seasonality.fall: Seedpods mature and split open, releasing clouds of fluffy seeds that drift on autumn breezes. Leaves may turn reddish before dying back.
seasonality.winter: Dies back completely to ground level, leaving only dried stems and empty seedpods that may persist into early winter.

funFact: The fluffy seeds of downy willowherb were once used as stuffing for pillows and mattresses by early New England settlers, earning some willowherbs the nickname "cotton grass" despite being completely unrelated to actual cotton.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other willowherbs, but the distinctly fuzzy, velvety texture of the entire plant sets downy willowherb apart - run your fingers along the stem and leaves, and you'll feel the difference immediately. Other willowherbs may have some hairs but lack this overall downy softness.
compareHints: Among New England's willowherbs, downy willowherb is distinguished by its thoroughly fuzzy texture - much more so than cinnamon willowherb or fringed willowherb. Great willowherb is much taller with showier flowers, while marsh willowherb has smoother, less hairy stems and grows in even wetter conditions. **Note: This species has very few confirmed observations in New England, so field identification should be made cautiously.**

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's willowherbs, cinnamon willowherb is distinguished by its colorful stems and leaves - most other willowherbs stay green throughout the season.
Among New England's willowherbs, great willowherb lives up to its name by being the tallest and most robust.
Among New England's willowherbs, fringed willowherb is distinguished by those characteristic tiny hairs along its leaf edges - no other local willowherb has this feature.
Unlike its lowland cousins like great willowherb or cinnamon willowherb, Hornemann's willowherb is much smaller in all respects - shorter stems, tinier flowers, and narrower leaves.
Among New England's willowherbs, linear-leaf willowherb has the narrowest leaves and prefers the wettest habitats.

Among New England willowherbs, hoary willowherb stands out for its overall grayish, densely fuzzy appearance - most other willowherbs like cinnamon willowherb or fringed willowherb are greener with less conspicuous hairs.
Marsh willowherb is much smaller and more delicate than Great Willowherb, which can tower over 6 feet tall with showy magenta flowers.
